definition: Oblivious means lacking consciousness or awareness of something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word oblivious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know oblivious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The seagull strutted across the picnic blanket, oblivious to three cats crouched at the garden's edge.
A distracted student misses a sentence when a phone buzzes; oblivious goes further - whole fire drills can pass unnoticed.
An inattentive guard still catches some of what passes the gate; the oblivious one perceives none of it - the word marks total failure to notice.

Unaware is the neutral, no-blame word for simply not knowing, because the information never came your way. Oblivious goes further: the facts are right in front of you — loud, posted, repeated — and your attention still never registers them at all.

Heedless people were warned and pushed on anyway; the word carries blame, because the warning reached them and they paid it no attention. Oblivious carries no such charge — an oblivious person never perceived the warning in the first place.

Untended, the old orchard slid into oblivion behind the new billboards.
Oblivious means lacking consciousness or awareness of something.
The new dishwasher, headphones snug, scrubbed a single stockpot to a mirror shine for ten straight minutes, oblivious to the ticket printer chattering out orders a foot behind his shoulder.
Oblivious is precise because his awareness simply never registers the printer - no choice, no defiance, just a total failure to notice.
Heedless would accuse him of brushing past a warning he had heard; oblivious says the sound never reached him at all.
Oblivious marks a total failure to notice - often comic, sometimes damning.
It points outward from the person: you are oblivious to the world.
Its mirror in this unit is obscurity, where the world fails to notice you.
Heedless is harsher: the heedless were warned and sailed on anyway.

On the morning the river burst its banks, Elias Grote sat in the window of the Corner Grind, editing a manuscript.
For two hours he was entirely oblivious to the scene beyond the glass: sirens, a loudspeaker truck making passes, neighbors stacking sandbags across the street.
The barista who finally tapped his shoulder said his name three times before he looked up.
'I remember thinking the light had gone strange,' he admitted later.
'I registered nothing else.' He had not chosen to ignore the warnings; as far as his attention was concerned, they had simply never happened.
